ORDER 1.
With the consent of learned counsel for the parties the matter is finally heard.

2. This petition under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. has been preferred by the petitioner/accused for quashing of FIR No.1110/2022 registered at Police Station Bhanwarkuwa, District Indore for offences punishable under Sections 376, 376(2)(n) and 506 of the IPC.
3. As per the prosecution, a report was lodged by the prosecutrix to the effect that in the year 2019-2020 she was studying in Barwani.
She was known to the petitioner.
He proposed to her after which they started talking.

On 05.12.2020 the petitioner called her to Indore and took her in his car from bus stand to a room of his friend and on the false pretext of marriage, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-IND:3818 2 MCRC-21446-2024 he committed rape upon her.
On the next day he sent her back to Barwani after which they used to talk to each other for some time.
Afterwards the petitioner again took her to the house of his friend.
On 15.03.2021 he called her to Indore permanently and they resided in a rented accommodation.
For a period of two years on the false pretext of marriage petitioner committed rape upon her.
On her asking he used to make some reason for not marrying her.
She refused all proposals which came to her for her marriage.

She Piyush Chouhan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 10 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/147302988/
1 informed her parents that she likes the petitioner and wants to marry him.

sentences.text: She had gone to Barwani for the marriage of her sister after which she came back to Indore but thereafter the petitioner started avoiding her.
Eventually he broke all contact with her and on 23.09.2022 he finally refused to marry her.

4. On lodging of the report by the prosecutrix investigation was commenced by the Police during course of which statements of witnesses were recorded and other material was collected and FIR has been registered against the petitioner.

5. This petition has been preferred by the petitioner on the ground that the allegations against him by the prosecutrix even if are taken to be true at their face value do not amount to commission of any offence by him.
It is not a case where the petitioner had developed physical relationship with the prosecutrix under false pretext of marriage.
It is at best a case of breach of promise to marry and cannot be in any manner stretched to be a case of false promise having been made to convince the prosecutrix to engage in sexual relations.
There is no misconception of fact which can be said to have NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-IND:3818 3 MCRC-21446-2024 vitiated the consent of prosecutrix.

The petitioner is alleged to have promised the prosecutrix that he would marry her which she accepted and thereafter only physical relationship was developed between them which continued for a considerable period of time.
The prosecutrix lived with the petitioner in a separate accommodation at Indore for a number of years.
Despite the petitioner not having married her she continued to have physical relationship with him.
She had even told her parents that she wants to marry the petitioner.
It is a simple case of love relationship between the parties which has gone wrong but, in any case, was not a case of commission of rape on false pretext of marriage.
It is hence submitted that the proceedings against the petitioner are gross abuse of process of law hence deserve to be quashed.

6. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents/State has strongly opposed the prayer and has submitted that from the allegations as levelled against the petitioner by the prosecutrix it is apparent that the same do constitute an offence having been committed by him.
The petitioner firstly promised the prosecutrix that he would marry her which was believed by her after only which she developed physical relationship with him.
The promise made by the petitioner was false to begin with and there was no intention on his part of marrying the prosecutrix.
The consent of the prosecutrix for physical relationship was hence obtained by the petitioner by false statement knowing it to be false since the inception.
7. Despite service of notice of this petition upon the prosecutrix there has not been any appearance on her part to oppose the same.

sentences.text: To appreciate the allegations as levelled by the prosecutrix against the accused it would be relevant to take note of the relevant judgments cited on part of the parties.

In Shambhu Kharwar (supra) it was held by the Supreme Court as under :-
"13.
In this backdrop and taking the allegations in the complaint as they stand, it is impossible to find in the FIR or in the charge-sheet, the essential ingredients of an offence under Section 376 IPC.

The crucial issue which is to be considered is whether the allegations indicate that the appellant had given a promise to the second respondent to marry which at the inception was false and on the basis of which the second respondent was induced into a sexual relationship.
Taking the allegations in the FIR and the charge-sheet as they stand, the crucial ingredients of the offence under Section 375 IPC are absent.
The relationship between the parties was purely of a consensual nature.

The relationship, as noted above, was in existence prior to the marriage of the second respondent and continued to subsist during the term of the marriage and after the second respondent was granted a divorce by mutual consent."
10.
In Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (supra) it was held that mere refusal to honor the promise of marriage and having sexual relationship on such promise by itself would not amount to commission of rape.

It was held as under :-
"14.
In the present case, the "misconception of fact" alleged by the complainant is the appellant's promise to marry her.

Specifically in the context of a promise to marry,
this Court has observed that there is a distinction between a false promise given on the understanding by the maker that it will be broken, and the breach of a promise which is made in good faith but subsequently not fulfilled.

In Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh (2019) 13 SCC 1 : this Court held :
"12.

The sum and substance of the aforesaid decisions would be that if it is established and proved that from the inception the accused who gave the promise to the prosecutrix to marry, did not have any intention to marry and the prosecutrix gave the consent for sexual intercourse on such an assurance by the accused that he would marry her, such a consent can be said to be a consent obtained on a misconception of fact as per Section 90 IPC and, in such a case, such a consent would not excuse the offender and such an offender can NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-IND:3818 5 MCRC-21446-2024 be said to have committed the rape as defined under Sections 375 IPC and can be convicted for the offence under Section 376 IPC."
Similar observations were made by this Court in Deepak Gulati v. State of Haryana (2013) 7 SCC 675 "21. ...

Thus, the court must examine whether there was made, at an early stage a false promise of marriage by the accused;"

sentences.text: When she asked the accused why he had spoiled her life, he promised to marry her.
On this premise, the accused repeatedly had sexual intercourse with the complainant.
When the complainant became pregnant, the accused refused to marry her.
When the matter was brought to the panchayat, the accused admitted to having had sexual intercourse with the complainant but subsequently absconded.

Given this factual background, the Court observed :
"10.

It appears that the intention of the accused as per the testimony of PW 1 was,
right from the beginning, not honest and he kept on promising that he will marry her,
till she became pregnant.

This kind of consent obtained by the accused cannot be said to be any consent because she was under a misconception of fact that the accused intends to marry her, therefore, she had submitted to sexual intercourse with him.
This fact is also admitted by the accused that he had committed sexual intercourse which is apparent from the testimony of PWs 1, 2 and 3 and before the panchayat of elders of the village.
It is more than clear that the accused made a false promise that he would marry her.

Therefore, the intention of the accused right from the beginning was not bona fide and the poor girl submitted to the lust of the accused, completely being misled by the accused who held out the promise for marriage.

This kind of consent taken by the accused with clear intention not to fulfil the promise and persuading the girl to believe that he is going to marry her and obtained her consent for the sexual intercourse under total misconception, cannot be treated to be a consent."
16.

Where the promise to marry is false and the intention of the maker at the time of making the promise itself was not to abide by it but to deceive the woman to convince her to engage in sexual relations, there is a "misconception of fact" that vitiates the woman's "consent".
On the other hand, a breach of a promise cannot be said to be a false promise.
To establish a false promise, the maker of the promise should have had no intention of upholding his word at the time of giving it.
The "consent" of a woman under Section 375 is vitiated on the ground of a "misconception of fact" where such misconception was the basis for her choosing to engage in the said act.

In Deepak Gulati v.
State of Haryana, (2013) 7 SCC 675 this Court observed :
"21. ...

There may be a case where the prosecutrix agrees to have sexual intercourse on account of her love and passion for the accused, and not solely on a c c o u n t o f m i s r e p r e s e n t a t i o n m a d e N E U T R A L C I T A T I O N N O .

sentences.text:
Hence, it is evident that there must be adequate evidence to show that at the relevant time i.e. at the initial stage itself, the accused had no intention whatsoever,
of keeping his promise to marry the victim.

There may, of course, be circumstances,
when a person having the best of intentions is unable to marry the victim owing to various unavoidable circumstances.
The "failure to keep a promise made with respect to a future uncertain date, due to reasons that are not very clear from the evidence available, does not always amount to misconception of fact.
In order to come within the meaning of the term "misconception of fact", the fact must have an immediate relevance".

Section 90 IPC cannot be called into aid in such a situation, to pardon the act of a girl in entirety, and fasten criminal liability on the other."
17. In Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003) 4 SCC 46 the complainant was a college-going student when the accused promised to marry her.

entities.text: Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003) 4 SCC 46
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the complainant's statement, she admitted that she was aware that there would be significant opposition from both the complainant's and accused's families to the proposed marriage.
She engaged in sexual intercourse with the accused but nonetheless kept the relationship secret from her family.

The Court observed that in these circumstances the accused's promise to marry the complainant was not of immediate relevance to the complainant's decision to engage in sexual intercourse with the accused, which was motivated by other factors :
"25.
There is yet another difficulty which faces the prosecution in this case.
In a case of this nature two conditions must be fulfilled for the application of Section 90 IPC.
Firstly, it must be shown that the consent was given under a misconception of fact.
Secondly, it must be proved that the person who obtained the consent knew, or had reason to believe that the consent was given in consequence of such misconception.
We have serious doubts that the promise to marry induced the prosecutrix to consent to having sexual intercourse with the appellant.
She knew, as we have observed earlier, that her marriage with the appellant was difficult on account of caste considerations.
The proposal was bound to meet with stiff opposition from members of both families.
There was therefore a distinct possibility, of which she was clearly conscious, that the marriage may not take place at all despite the promise of the appellant.

The question still remains whether even if it were so, the appellant knew,
or had reason to believe, that the prosecutrix had consented to having sexual intercourse with him only as a consequence of her belief, based on his promise, that they will get married in due course.
There is hardly any evidence to prove this fact.

On the contrary, the circumstances of the case tend to support the conclusion that the appellant had reason to believe that the consent given by the prosecutrix was the result of their deep love for each other.
It is not disputed that they were deeply in love.
They met often, and it does appear that the prosecutrix permitted him liberties which, if at all, are permitted only to a person with whom one is in deep love.
It is also not without significance that the prosecutrix stealthily went out with the appellant NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-IND:3818 7 MCRC-21446-2024 to a lonely place at 12 o'clock in the night.
It usually happens in such cases, when two young persons are madly in love, that they promise to each other several times that come what may, they will get married."

18. To summarise the legal position that Piyush Chouhan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 10 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/147302988/
5 emerges from the above cases, the "consent"
of a woman with respect to Section 375 must involve an active and reasoned deliberation towards the proposed act.

To establish whether the "consent" was vitiated by a "misconception of fact"
arising out of a promise to marry, two propositions must be established.
The promise of marriage must have been a false promise, given in bad faith and with no intention of being adhered to at the time it was given.

The false promise itself must be of immediate relevance, or bear a direct nexus to the woman's decision to engage in the sexual act."
11.

When the facts of the present case are examined in the light of the aforesaid dictum it has to be ascertained whether the promise of marriage given by the petitioner was a false promise, given in bad faith and with no intention of being adhered to at the time it was given.
The facts reveal that the prosecutrix was known to the petitioner since prior to 2019-2020.
The petitioner had stated that he wants to marry her.
On his asking the prosecutrix had come to Indore and had gone along with him to a room of his friend.
They had physical relationship over there.

Though it is contended that the petitioner had promised the prosecutrix that he would marry her and only for that reason she gave her consent but it is to be observed that thereafter the prosecutrix went back to Barwani and continued talking to the petitioner.
She came back to Indore on 2-3 occasions and had physical relationship with him.
Subsequently, on 15.03.2021 she came back to Indore and lived together with the petitioner for a period of two years.
During all this period she continued to have physical relationship with him despite him not marrying her.
If the petitioner was not marrying her then her natural conduct would have been to stop having physical relationship with him.
However, she did not do so.

The relationship of the petitioner and the NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-IND:3818 8 MCRC-21446-2024 prosecutrix continued for a period of about three years.
12. It is not the allegation of the prosecutrix that when the initial promise to marry was given by the petitioner it was false at the very inception.
She herself states that she was in love with the petitioner who had promised to marry her.
The relationship between the petitioner and prosecutrix was purely of a consensual nature.
The same had its inception in a love affair between them.
The promise made by the petitioner of marrying the prosecutrix cannot in the facts and circumstances of the case be said to have been given with no intention of honoring it.
13. On the record is a statement given by the prosecutrix on 22.10.2022 at Police Station Bhanwarkuwa, District Indore which is just 10 days prior to the lodging of the complaint by her.
In that statement she herself stated that she had developed physical relationship with the petitioner out of her own consent.
She stated that she wants to marry the petitioner and wants to give him a period of 7 days for the same.
Learned counsel for the respondents/State was directed to ascertain as to whether the aforesaid statement was given by the prosecutrix.
However, there is no confirmation of the said fact and it is stated that the record is not traceable.
However, from the statement it is observed that there is seal of Police Station Bhanwarkuwa and signatures of the prosecutrix.
There is no reason to disbelieve the same particularly when prosecutrix has not denied it.
From the statement itself it is evident that the prosecutrix wanted to marry the petitioner till 10 days prior to lodging of the FIR by her.

She admitted that her physical relationship with the Piyush Chouhan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 10 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/147302988/
6 petitioner was with her consent.

Thus, in view of the aforesaid discussion, even if the allegations as levelled by the prosecutrix against the petitioner are taken to be true at their face value it cannot be said that any offence has been committed by the petitioner.

The petition hence deserves to be and is accordingly allowed and FIR No.1110/2022 registered at Police Station Bhanwarkuwa, District Indore against the petitioner for offences punishable under Section 376, 376(2)(n) and 506 of the IPC is hereby quashed and so are the consequential proceedings taken pursuant thereto.
